lessons.title: Probability Predictions
lessons.summary: How classifiers output probabilities, not just labels: P(y=k|x), the sigmoid and softmax, thresholds that convert probabilities into decisions, how different models estimate probabilities, uncertainty and calibration (Platt/isotonic/temperature), and probability-sensitive metrics (log loss, Brier score).

content.text: What a probability prediction is

Most classifiers don't just say “spam” or “not spam.” Underneath, they produce a number — how sure they are. A probability prediction is that number: a value between 0 and 1 estimating how likely a particular class is for a given observation.
A model output between 0 and 1 that represents the model's estimated likelihood that a particular outcome or class is true for a given observation.

content.explanation: Read as: “the probability that the class is k, given the input features x.”

content.caption: Figure 1. A probability communicates uncertainty on a scale from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain).

content.text: A probability is not a guarantee. A prediction of 0.80 means that among many similar cases, a well-calibrated model should be right about 80% of the time — not that this single case is definitely positive.
content.title: Important

content.text: Probability vs class prediction

rows: The final category after a rule.

content.caption: Figure 2. The probability is an intermediate output; a threshold or decision rule turns it into an action.

content.text: Keep two stages separate in your mind: the model estimates a probability, and a decision policy converts that probability into an action. They are related but distinct.
content.title: Two stages

content.text: Binary probability predictions
Binary classification has two classes, usually written 0 and 1. The model predicts the probability of class 1, and the other class simply gets whatever is left over:

content.expression: p = P(y = 1 | x)     and     P(y = 0 | x) = 1 − p
content.explanation: The two probabilities always add up to 1.

content.text: Logistic regression and the sigmoid
Logistic regression first computes a real-valued score z from the features, then squeezes that score into the 0–1 range with the sigmoid function.

content.explanation: A plain weighted sum — it can be any real number.
The sigmoid maps that score to a probability between 0 and 1.

content.caption: Figure 3. The sigmoid smoothly converts any real-valued score into a probability; z = 0 gives exactly 0.50.

content.text: Positive z → probability above 0.50; negative z → below 0.50; z = 0 → exactly 0.50. Larger absolute scores usually mean greater confidence.
content.title: Reading the score

content.text: Worked example: will a student pass?
A simplified model uses weekly study hours x with the equation z = −3 + 0.5x, then applies the sigmoid.
For x = 10: z = −3 + 0.5(10) = 2, and the sigmoid gives p = 1 / (1 + exp(−2)) ≈ 0.881 — an 88.1% estimated chance of passing.
content.title: Worked calculation

content.text: From probability to a decision: thresholds
A decision threshold t is the cut-off that turns a probability into a hard label:

content.expression: Predict class 1 if p ≥ t; otherwise predict class 0.
content.explanation: Everything at or above the threshold becomes a positive; everything below becomes a negative.

content.caption: Figure 4. With t = 0.50, probabilities on the left become class 0 and those on the right become class 1.

content.text: 0.50 is not always the right threshold

rows: More positives; higher recall; more false positives.
Missing a positive is costly (e.g. safety screening).
Balances classes only under certain assumptions.
Costs and class frequencies are roughly balanced.
Fewer positives; higher precision; more false negatives.
A positive action needs strong evidence.

content.caption: Figure 5. Precision and recall usually move in opposite directions as the threshold changes.

content.text: Same probabilities, different decisions
The probabilities below never change — only the threshold does, and that alone flips several labels.
The model probabilities stay fixed; only the decision policy changes. Treat probability modelling and decision-making as related but separate stages.
content.title: Main lesson

content.text: Multiclass probability predictions
Multiclass classification has more than two mutually exclusive classes. The model outputs one probability per class, and they should sum to 1:

content.explanation: A valid probability distribution across all K classes.

content.caption: Figure 6. The largest probability is 0.73 for Dog, so the argmax prediction is Dog.

content.text: The softmax function
A multiclass model produces one score zₖ per class. Softmax converts those scores into a probability distribution:

content.expression: P(y = k | x) = exp(zₖ) / Σⱼ exp(zⱼ)
content.explanation: Exponentiate each score, then normalise so everything sums to 1.

content.text: The hard prediction is usually the class with the largest probability — predicted class = argmaxₖ P(y = k | x) — but this rule hides how close the runner-up was.
content.title: Argmax rule

content.text: Confidence and margin
The top-two margin (top probability minus second-highest) tells you how decisive the choice really is.
How common classifiers produce probabilities

rows: Can be miscalibrated if the model is misspecified.
Strong independence can create extreme confidence.
Small leaves give unstable, extreme probabilities.
Better than one tree, but still check calibration.
Logistic/softmax link on the ensemble score.
Fraction of the k neighbours per class.
Resolution limited by k (k=5 → steps of 0.20).
Native output is a margin; needs Platt scaling.
Never treat the raw decision score as a probability.

content.text: Example: a tree leaf's probability
A decision-tree leaf holds 20 training observations: 15 positive and 5 negative.

content.explanation: The leaf's class proportions become the predicted probabilities.

content.text: A pure leaf with just 2 positive examples may output 1.00, but that rests on almost no evidence. Minimum leaf size, pruning, smoothing, or calibration make such outputs more reliable.
content.title: Caution

content.text: Uncertainty in probability outputs

content.caption: Figure 7. Where the two class probability distributions overlap, cases are genuinely hard to separate.

rows: Still verify calibration and out-of-distribution risk.
Consider human review or more information.
Inspect the top classes and the margin.

content.text: Aleatoric vs epistemic uncertainty

rows: Noise inherent in the data; more data won't remove it.
A blurry image truly resembles both cat and dog.
From limited model knowledge; better data can reduce it.
The model meets a device type absent from training.

content.text: A single softmax probability mainly expresses relative confidence; it does not automatically separate aleatoric from epistemic uncertainty.
content.title: Practical note

content.text: Probability calibration
Calibration asks whether predicted probabilities match real-world frequencies. A calibrated model that says 0.70 for many cases should see roughly 70% positives among them.

content.caption: Figure 8. On a reliability diagram, points near the diagonal indicate good calibration; points below it indicate overconfidence.

rows: Predictions too close to the centre.

content.text: Calibration methods

rows: Fit a logistic function mapping scores to probabilities.
Simple; good when the distortion is sigmoid-shaped.
More flexible, but needs more data and can overfit.
Divide logits by one learned temperature.
Common for neural nets; keeps the class ranking.

content.text: Fit the base model on training data, fit the calibrator on separate validation/CV predictions, and evaluate on untouched test data. Never calibrate on the test set.
content.title: Correct workflow

content.text: Evaluating probability predictions
Accuracy only checks whether the final class is right. Probability-sensitive metrics also judge confidence — rewarding confident correct predictions and punishing confident wrong ones.
Log loss (cross-entropy)

content.expression: Binary log loss = −[ y log(p) + (1 − y) log(1 − p) ]
content.explanation: Lower is better; it grows sharply for confident mistakes.

content.text: Log loss heavily penalises confident mistakes. Predicting 0.01 for an outcome that actually happens is far worse than predicting 0.40.
content.title: Key property

content.text: Brier score

content.explanation: The mean squared difference between predicted probability and actual outcome.

content.caption: Figure 9. Both Brier score and log loss prefer probabilities closer to the truth; log loss rises more sharply for confident errors.

content.text: Threshold-dependent vs threshold-independent

rows: Quality of class decisions at a chosen threshold.
Counts of true/false positives and negatives.
Ranking positives above negatives across thresholds.
Precision–recall ranking, great for rare positives.

content.text: Choosing a threshold for a real task
Threshold selection should follow the objective and the cost of errors — not habit. A practical process:

items: Clarify which error is more costly: a false positive or a false negative.
Generate validation-set probabilities without touching the test set.
Evaluate candidate thresholds by precision, recall, F1, expected cost, or capacity limits.
Choose the threshold that best meets the operational requirement.
Lock the threshold and report final performance on the test set.
Monitor class balance and calibration after deployment.

content.text: Cost-sensitive example
Suppose a safety-screening system treats a missed positive as five times costlier than an unnecessary alert. We compare thresholds by an illustrative cost = 5×FN + 1×FP.
Threshold 0.30 has the lowest cost (50) here, despite more false positives — because missed positives are expensive. The “best” threshold always depends on the cost model.
content.title: Best threshold here

content.text: Practical Python workflow
In scikit-learn, classifiers that support probabilities provide predict_proba(). In a binary task the second column is usually the probability of class 1 — but always confirm with model.classes_.

content.code:
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import log_loss, brier_score_loss

model = LogisticRegression()
model.fit(X_train, y_train)

# Probability of each class (confirm the column order with model.classes_)
proba_matrix = model.predict_proba(X_test)
p_positive = proba_matrix[:, 1]

# Convert probabilities into labels using a chosen threshold
threshold = 0.40
y_pred = (p_positive >= threshold).astype(int)

# Probability-sensitive evaluation
print("Log loss:", log_loss(y_test, p_positive))
print("Brier score:", brier_score_loss(y_test, p_positive))

content.text: predict() returns hard labels, predict_proba() returns probabilities, and decision_function() returns raw scores/margins — which are not probabilities. Always map each probability column to model.classes_; column 0 is not automatically “negative.”
content.title: Common API mistake

content.text: Common mistakes

rows: Margins and logits aren't calibrated probabilities.
Use a probability link or calibration.
The best threshold depends on costs and balance.
Tune the threshold on validation data.
Add log loss, Brier score and calibration.
Models can be overconfident on new data.
The same column may mean different classes.
Keep full precision; round only for display.

content.text: Mini case study: email spam probability
A binary classifier predicts the probability that each email is spam. The organisation wants high recall (dangerous messages should rarely reach users) while controlling unnecessary blocking.
Tallying the outcomes at each threshold shows the trade-off directly:
Lowering the threshold from 0.50 to 0.30 catches all spam (recall → 1.00) but wrongly blocks one legitimate email (precision → 0.75). The probability outputs make this policy trade-off visible.
content.title: Interpretation

content.text: Revision

items: A probability prediction is a number from 0 to 1 estimating how likely a class is for an input.
Binary classifiers output P(y=1 | x); the other class gets 1 − p.
Multiclass classifiers output a probability vector that sums to 1.
A threshold converts a probability into a label, but 0.50 isn't always best.
Lower thresholds usually raise recall; higher thresholds usually raise precision.
Calibration asks whether stated probabilities match observed frequencies.
Log loss and Brier score judge probability quality, not just final labels.
Raw scores, margins and logits are not automatically probabilities.
Probability evaluation, threshold selection and final testing need properly separated data.

content.text: Key formula sheet

rows: P(y = k | x) = exp(zₖ) / Σⱼ exp(zⱼ)

content.text: Glossary

rows: Agreement between predicted probabilities and observed frequencies.
Strength of a model's preference, often the top predicted probability.
The cut-off converting a probability into a label.
A real-valued score before the sigmoid; log(p/(1−p)).
A plot of predicted-probability bins vs observed positive rates.
Converts multiclass scores into probabilities summing to 1.
A loss rewarding honest probabilities (log loss, Brier).
Lack of certainty about the outcome or model knowledge.

A margin is an unbounded relative score; it needs a probability mapping or calibration.
It would leak information and give optimistically biased estimates.

keyPoints: A probability prediction is a 0–1 estimate of how likely a class is; binary gives P(y=1|x) with the other class 1−p, multiclass a vector summing to 1.
The sigmoid maps a score to a binary probability; softmax maps scores to a multiclass distribution.
A threshold turns a probability into a label — 0.50 isn't always best; lower raises recall, higher raises precision.
Calibration checks whether stated probabilities match observed frequencies; fit calibrators on validation data, never the test set.

lessons.title: Classification Thresholds
lessons.summary: The cut-off that turns probabilities into decisions: the decision rule, how moving the threshold trades false positives against false negatives, threshold-dependent metrics and confusion matrices, ROC/PR curves, cost-sensitive and constraint-based selection on validation data, calibration, and multiclass/multilabel thresholds.

content.text: What a classification threshold is

A classifier rarely hands you a clean “yes” or “no.” It gives a score — a probability that an example belongs to the positive class. The threshold is the cut-off that turns that score into an actual decision. Set it, and every probability above it becomes a positive, everything below a negative.
The cut-off value used to convert a model's predicted score or probability into a class decision.

content.expression: Predict positive class if  P(y = 1 | x) ≥ threshold
content.explanation: Otherwise predict the negative class. 0.50 is a common default — but not automatically the best choice for every problem.

content.caption: Figure 1. A probability only becomes a class after a threshold is applied — here everything above 0.50 is predicted spam.

rows: Model's confidence it's the positive class.

content.text: Why thresholds matter

The model produces a continuous score; the threshold decides where that score splits into two actions. So changing only the threshold can change the predictions — even when the trained model itself is untouched.

items: Lower threshold → more cases labelled positive.
Higher threshold → fewer cases labelled positive.
The ranking of examples never changes — only the cut-off on the score moves.
Threshold selection is a decision-policy problem, not just a model-training one.

content.caption: Figure 2. Sliding the threshold changes how many examples receive the positive label.

content.text: Worked example: email spam
An email classifier outputs a spam probability. For each email, apply the rule “probability ≥ threshold means spam.” Here is what happens at threshold 0.50:
At threshold 0.50, an email at 0.48 is predicted “not spam” while one at 0.51 is predicted “spam.” The threshold forces a sharp decision even when the two probabilities are almost identical.
content.title: Reading the table

content.text: Thresholds and the confusion matrix
Every threshold produces its own confusion matrix. The four possible outcomes are:

content.caption: Figure 3. The confusion matrix produced by the example data at threshold 0.50.

content.text: Threshold-dependent metrics

rows: How many actual positives are detected.
How many actual negatives are correctly rejected.

content.text: Comparing three thresholds
Run the same model at three thresholds and every metric shifts. The table transposes the results so you can read each metric across the thresholds.

items: At 0.30, the system catches nearly all spam but blocks more legitimate email.
At 0.70, it blocks fewer legitimate emails but lets more spam through.
At 0.50, the trade-off is intermediate — whether that's acceptable depends on the cost.

content.caption: Figure 4. Precision, recall, specificity and F1-score all change as the threshold moves.

content.text: The core trade-off: false positives vs false negatives

rows: Recall usually rises; precision/specificity may fall.
Precision/specificity may rise; recall usually falls.

content.text: There is rarely a universally “best” threshold. The right one is whichever makes its errors match the real-world priorities and constraints of the task.
content.title: Key principle

content.text: Application examples

rows: Missing a case is dangerous; confirmatory tests can follow.
A low threshold catches more fraud but can flood investigators.
Blocking an important email may be worse than letting some spam through.
Early warning is worth it when equipment damage is costly.

content.text: Choosing a threshold systematically
Threshold selection belongs on validation data, never the final test set. A practical procedure:

items: Define the positive class and the action a positive prediction triggers.
Identify the relative cost of false positives vs false negatives.
Generate model probabilities on a validation dataset.
Evaluate a range of thresholds, e.g. 0.05 to 0.95.
Compute the required metrics and operational volume at each threshold.
Choose the threshold that meets the objective and constraints.
Lock it, evaluate once on the test set, then monitor after deployment.

content.caption: Figure 5. The recommended threshold-selection workflow.

content.text: Common threshold objectives

rows: Pick the threshold with the highest validation F1 or balanced accuracy.
Pick the highest threshold still giving recall ≥ 0.95.
Pick a threshold with FPR below an operational limit.
Pick the threshold with the lowest weighted FP+FN cost.
Pick a threshold producing no more alerts than staff can review.

content.text: ROC and precision–recall curves
Instead of reporting one threshold, a curve summarises performance across many possible thresholds at once.
ROC curve

items: Plots the true positive rate (recall) against the false positive rate.
Each point corresponds to a different threshold.
Useful for understanding the sensitivity–specificity trade-off.

content.caption: Figure 6. Every point on the ROC curve corresponds to a different threshold (t = 0.3, 0.5, 0.7 marked).

content.text: Precision–recall curve

items: Plots precision against recall across thresholds.
Often more informative when the positive class is rare, since it focuses on positive predictions.

content.text: AUC summarises ranking quality across all thresholds, but deployment still requires picking one concrete threshold and checking its confusion matrix and operational effects.
content.title: Important

content.text: Cost-sensitive threshold selection
When you can estimate error costs, compute the expected decision cost at each threshold and pick the cheapest.

content.expression: Total cost = (FP × cost of FP) + (FN × cost of FN)
content.explanation: Weight each error type by how much it actually hurts.

content.text: Suppose each false positive costs 1 unit of effort and each false negative costs 5 units, because missed spam is more harmful:

Here the lowest-cost threshold is 0.30 (cost 12), despite more false positives — because missed spam is five times as costly. In real projects, error costs should be set with domain experts and reviewed regularly.
content.title: Best in this example

content.text: Calibration and thresholds
Thresholds are easiest to interpret when probabilities are calibrated. A calibrated model that predicts 0.70 for many similar cases should be right about 70% of the time for them.

items: Good ranking does not guarantee good probability calibration.
A threshold like 0.80 has a meaningful risk interpretation only when probabilities are reasonably calibrated.
Assess calibration with reliability diagrams and metrics such as the Brier score.
Calibration must be learned and checked on data separate from the final test evaluation.

content.text: Don't assume a score of 0.90 always means a true 90% probability. Some models produce scores useful for ranking but poorly calibrated as probabilities.
content.title: Practical warning

content.text: Thresholds beyond binary

rows: Highest probability; optionally require max ≥ t.
One confidence threshold or per-class rejection.
For each label j: p(label j) ≥ tⱼ.
One global threshold or a separate one per label.

content.text: In single-label multiclass, argmax usually picks the top class — but you can add a confidence threshold: if the highest probability falls below it, return “uncertain,” “other,” or request human review. In multilabel problems each label is independent, so an image might get “car” at 0.50 and “night” at 0.35; per-label thresholds help when labels differ in frequency or cost.
Common mistakes

items: Using 0.50 without justification — it may not match class imbalance, costs, or capacity.
Choosing the threshold on test data — this leaks information and inflates reported performance.
Optimising only accuracy — it can hide poor recall or precision on imbalanced classes.
Ignoring alert volume — a strong threshold may create more cases than staff can process.
Ignoring calibration — a risk-based threshold is unreliable when probabilities are miscalibrated.
Never revisiting the threshold — drift, changed costs, and shifting prevalence make old thresholds unsuitable.

content.text: Quick revision

rows: A cut-off converting a score/probability into a class decision.
More positives; recall often rises; false positives often rise.
Fewer positives; precision/specificity may rise; false negatives often rise.
No — it's only a default and must be validated for the task.
On validation data, using a pre-defined objective or constraint.
Confusion matrices, metric-vs-threshold plots, ROC and PR curves, cost analysis.
Threshold, confusion matrix, metrics, selection rule, operational impact.

content.text: The trained classifier produces scores; the threshold turns those scores into actions. Lower thresholds favour detecting more positives; higher thresholds favour avoiding false alarms. A defensible threshold is chosen on validation data by matching metrics, costs, capacity and risk to the real decision.
content.title: Remember

content.text: Practice questions

items: A model gives probability 0.63 and the threshold is 0.70. What class is predicted? → Negative, because 0.63 < 0.70.
A team wants to detect almost every positive case. Which way should the threshold move? → Lower, while watching the rise in false positives.
Why should the test set not be used to choose the threshold? → Because tuning on test data leaks information and biases the final evaluation.
Which metric matters most when missing a positive is especially costly? → Recall/sensitivity, with the false-negative count and cost.
What must be monitored after deployment? → Class prevalence, score distribution, calibration, errors, workload and real-world cost.

keyPoints: A threshold converts a predicted probability into a class decision; changing it changes predictions without retraining the model.
Lower thresholds raise recall (more false positives); higher thresholds raise precision/specificity (more false negatives).
Every threshold has its own confusion matrix and metrics — there is rarely one universally best value.
Select the threshold on validation data by an objective or constraint (min recall, min precision, lowest cost, workload limit), never on the test set.
Thresholds are only meaningful as risk levels when probabilities are calibrated; per-label thresholds suit multilabel problems.
commonMistakes: Using 0.50 without justifying it for the task.
Choosing or tuning the threshold on the test set.
Optimising accuracy alone and ignoring recall/precision or alert volume.
Treating an uncalibrated score as a true probability.

lessons.title: Class Imbalance
lessons.summary: Why skewed classes break accuracy and how to fix it: majority/minority classes and the imbalance ratio, the accuracy trap, imbalance-aware metrics (recall, precision, F1, balanced accuracy, MCC, PR-AUC), data/algorithm/decision-level treatments (oversampling, undersampling, SMOTE/ADASYN, class weights, balanced ensembles, threshold tuning), and leakage-safe resampling.

content.text: What class imbalance is

Class imbalance happens when the classes in a dataset contain very different numbers of examples. The class with more observations is the majority class; the one with fewer is the minority class — and it's often the minority class that matters most.
A classification setting where the target classes contain very different numbers of observations, so one (the minority class) is much rarer than another (the majority class).
Take a fraud-detection dataset of 1,000 transactions: 950 legitimate and 50 fraudulent. Legitimate makes up 95% of the data and fraud just 5% — a classic imbalanced binary problem.

content.caption: The fraud example: 950 legitimate (95%) versus 50 fraud (5%) observations.

content.text: Imbalance is not automatically a problem. It becomes one when the model learns the majority class well but fails to detect the minority class that actually matters.
content.title: Main idea

content.text: This lesson stays focused on class imbalance in classification — its effects, how to evaluate it, and how to treat it.
content.title: Scope

content.text: Measuring the imbalance

content.expression: Imbalance Ratio (IR) = majority examples ÷ minority examples
content.explanation: For 950 legitimate and 50 fraud cases: IR = 950 ÷ 50 = 19, i.e. a 19:1 imbalance.

content.caption: Figure 1. A conceptual feature-space view: the minority class simply has far fewer points to learn from.

rows: One or more classes have far fewer examples.
The model may mainly learn majority patterns.
Often meaningful when costs are similar.
Can look high even when the minority is ignored.
Minority detection, error cost, metric choice.
Fraud, disease, faults, rare events, churn.

content.text: Where imbalance appears

items: Binary: one class is much rarer than the other — fraud vs legitimate.
Multiclass: one or several classes have very few examples — rare machine-failure types.
Multilabel: some labels occur very rarely even when others are common.

rows: Fraudulent transactions are rare, but missing them is costly.
A serious disease may affect only a small percentage of patients.
Most products are normal; defective items are uncommon.
Attacks are rare compared with normal network traffic.
Far fewer customers leave than stay.
Default cases are often fewer than non-default.
Harmful messages are a small share of all messages.

content.text: How severe is the imbalance?
There's no universal ratio that automatically defines a serious problem. Severity depends on the number of minority examples, class overlap, noise, the model, and the cost of each error type.

rows: Often needs weighting, threshold work, or resampling.
May need anomaly-detection ideas or more data.

content.text: A 60:40 split can still be hard if classes overlap strongly, while a 95:5 split may be learnable if the classes are clearly separated and enough minority examples exist. Ratio isn't the whole story.
content.title: Important

content.text: Why imbalance causes problems
Several forces push a model toward ignoring the minority class:

items: Majority-class bias: minimising average error can be achieved by mostly predicting the majority class.
Too few minority patterns: the model may not see enough variety, and rare points can look like noise.
Decision-boundary shift: the boundary drifts toward the minority, enlarging the majority region.
Poor calibration: predicted probabilities may not reflect real risk, especially after aggressive resampling.
Unequal error costs: missing a fraud or disease case is often far worse than a false alarm.

content.caption: Figure 2. A majority-only classifier can score high accuracy while detecting none of the minority cases — an imbalance-aware model trades a little accuracy for real minority recall.

content.text: The accuracy trap
Consider 1,000 cases: 950 negative, 50 positive. A lazy model predicts every case as negative.

items: Accuracy = (TP + TN) / Total = (0 + 950) / 1,000 = 95%.
Positive-class recall = TP / (TP + FN) = 0 / 50 = 0%.
The model misses every positive case — yet reports 95% accuracy.

content.text: Accuracy alone is unsafe for imbalanced classification. Always examine the confusion matrix and class-specific metrics.
content.title: Conclusion

content.text: Evaluation metrics for imbalance
The recommended metrics, split into what they measure and when to reach for them:

rows: How many actual positives were found.
How many predicted positives were right.
How many negatives were correctly rejected.
Overall quality from all four cells.
Can be inflated by many false alarms.
May drop when recall is pushed up.
One score for the positive class.
Can hide poor positive recall alone.
Harsh when tiny classes are noisy.

items: Count observations in each target class.
Calculate class percentages and the imbalance ratio.
Visualise the target distribution with a count plot or bar chart.
Inspect class counts separately in train, validation, and test sets.
Use stratified splitting so each split keeps similar class proportions.
Check whether the minority class has mislabeled, duplicated, or low-quality examples.
Study feature overlap and class-wise performance, not only target counts.

percentages = y.value_counts(normalize=True).mul(100)

print("Counts:")

content.text: Methods for handling imbalance
The best treatment depends on the dataset, model, evaluation objective, and error cost. Methods fall into data-level, algorithm-level, and decision-level groups.
Data-level methods

items: Random oversampling: duplicate minority examples until classes are less skewed — simple, keeps all majority data, but repeated records can overfit.
Random undersampling: drop majority examples — faster and lighter, but useful information may be lost.
SMOTE: create synthetic minority points between nearby minority observations rather than exact copies — better coverage, but unreliable when classes overlap or are noisy.
ADASYN: focus synthetic data on harder-to-learn minority regions — targets difficult areas but can amplify noise.
Cleaning (Tomek Links, Edited Nearest Neighbours): remove ambiguous or overlapping points, often combined with oversampling for cleaner boundaries.

content.caption: Figure 3. Oversampling grows the minority class; undersampling shrinks the majority class.

content.text: Algorithm-level methods

items: Class weights / cost-sensitive learning: penalise minority mistakes more. Many models support class_weight='balanced', raising minority influence without touching the records.
Specialised ensembles: Balanced Random Forest, EasyEnsemble and RUSBoost combine sampling with ensembling — strong on difficult tabular imbalance.
Loss functions: focal loss down-weights easy majority examples and focuses on hard cases — common in deep learning like object detection.

content.expression: balanced class weight ∝ Total samples ÷ (Number of classes × Samples in that class)
content.explanation: Smaller classes get larger weights, so their errors count for more during training.

content.text: Decision-level: threshold tuning

A classifier usually turns a probability into a class using a 0.50 threshold, but you can change it to match the objective. Lowering it typically raises recall (at some precision cost); raising it typically raises precision (at some recall cost).

content.caption: Figure 4. The precision–recall trade-off as the decision threshold changes.

rows: Fast; less memory and training time.
Can create overlap or unrealistic samples.
No synthetic data; easy to use.

content.text: Correct workflow: avoid leakage

Resampling must happen only on training data. If synthetic or duplicated minority examples are created before the train–test split, nearly identical information leaks into both sets — producing unrealistically high results.

rows: Never resample or fit preprocessing on the test set.
Preprocessing, resampling and model in one pipeline.
Resampling happens separately inside each fold.
Report on the real, untouched class distribution.

content.text: Never apply SMOTE to the full dataset before splitting. The test set must represent unseen, real-world data at its natural prevalence.
content.title: Leakage warning

content.text: Practical Python pipeline
A leakage-safe pipeline — SMOTE is applied only inside training, and the test set stays untouched.

content.code:
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import (
    classification_report,
    confusion_matrix,
    average_precision_score
)
from imblearn.over_sampling import SMOTE
from imblearn.pipeline import Pipeline

# 1. Split BEFORE resampling
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y,
    test_size=0.20,
    stratify=y,
    random_state=42
)

# 2. Resampling lives INSIDE the pipeline
pipeline = Pipeline(steps=[
    ("scale", StandardScaler()),
    ("smote", SMOTE(random_state=42)),
    ("model", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))
])

# 3. Fit only on training data
pipeline.fit(X_train, y_train)

# 4. Evaluate on untouched test data
y_pred = pipeline.predict(X_test)
y_prob = pipeline.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]

print(confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred))
print(classification_report(y_test, y_pred))
print("PR-AUC:", average_precision_score(y_test, y_prob))

Often simpler than synthetic sampling: just tell the model to weight the minority more heavily.

model = LogisticRegression(
    class_weight="balanced",
    max_iter=1000,
    random_state=42
)

Can look strong at very low prevalence.

High accuracy does not guarantee good minority detection.
Always inspect the confusion matrix and class-specific metrics.
Recall focuses on missed positives; precision focuses on false alarms.

Choose the best method via cross-validation and the real cost of errors.

lessons.title: Confusion Matrix
lessons.summary: The table behind every classification metric: the four outcomes (TP/TN/FP/FN), all metrics derived from it (accuracy, precision, recall, specificity, F1, NPV, FPR/FNR), a full worked email-spam example, the accuracy trap under imbalance, threshold effects, multiclass matrices with one-vs-rest and macro/micro/weighted averaging, and normalized matrices.

content.text: What a confusion matrix is

A single accuracy number tells you how often a model is right — but not how it goes wrong. A confusion matrix fills that gap. It's a small table that lines up what actually happened against what the model predicted, so you can see exactly which cases it caught and which it confused.
A table that summarises a classifier's performance by comparing its predicted class labels against the true (actual) class labels.

items: Rows usually represent actual classes; columns represent predicted classes — but some tools flip this, so always read the axis labels.
Diagonal cells hold correct predictions.
Off-diagonal cells hold errors — confusions between classes.
For binary classification there are four outcomes: TP, TN, FP and FN.

content.text: A confusion matrix is not itself a single score. It's a table of counts from which many performance measures are calculated.
content.title: Key idea

content.text: Why it's useful

items: It shows what kinds of mistakes the model makes, not just how many.
It separates positive-class performance from negative-class performance.
It supports metric choice based on the real cost of each error type.
It helps compare models, thresholds and data-preparation choices.

content.text: The four outcomes in binary classification

rows: Raises a false alarm (Type I error).
Misses a real positive case (Type II error).

content.text: Read each term in two parts. The second word (positive/negative) is what the model predicted; the first word (true/false) is whether that prediction was correct.
content.title: Memory rule

content.text: Error costs in practice
Which error hurts more depends entirely on the application:

rows: Healthy person flagged for extra tests.

content.text: Worked example: email spam
A test set has 100 emails, with “spam” as the positive class. The model's results:

items: 35 spam emails correctly classified as spam (TP = 35).
50 legitimate emails correctly classified as not spam (TN = 50).
5 legitimate emails wrongly classified as spam (FP = 5).
10 spam emails wrongly classified as legitimate (FN = 10).

content.caption: Figure 1. The worked binary confusion matrix for 100 emails (TN = 50, FP = 5, FN = 10, TP = 35).

content.explanation: Every case lands in exactly one of the four cells.

content.text: The model makes 85 correct and 15 incorrect predictions — but more tellingly, it misses 10 spam emails while wrongly blocking only 5 legitimate ones.

content.text: Metrics from the matrix
Each metric below is calculated straight from the four cells, using the worked example's numbers.
Accuracy and error rate

content.explanation: The proportion of all predictions that are correct.
Simply 1 − Accuracy.

content.text: Accuracy is most informative when classes are reasonably balanced and false positives and false negatives matter about equally.
content.title: Use with care

content.text: Precision and recall

content.explanation: Of all cases predicted positive, how many really were? High precision = few false alarms.
Of all actual positives, how many did the model find? High recall = few missed positives.

items: Precision matters when a false positive is costly.
Recall matters when a false negative is costly.

content.text: Specificity, F1 and NPV

content.explanation: Of all actual negatives, how many were correctly rejected?
The harmonic mean — it drops low if either precision or recall is weak, so a single bad value can't hide.
Of all cases predicted negative, how many really were negative?

content.text: Error rates

content.explanation: FPR = 1 − Specificity; FNR = 1 − Recall.

items: Confirm which class is treated as positive.
Check the axis orientation: actual vs predicted.
Check the total number of observations.
Inspect the diagonal cells for correct predictions.
Inspect FP and FN separately — don't combine them too early.
Decide which error carries the greater real-world cost.
Calculate the metric that matches that cost.
Compare against a baseline and other models or thresholds.
Check whether class imbalance makes overall accuracy unreliable.

content.text: Don't ask only “What is the accuracy?” Ask “Which cases does the model miss, which does it wrongly flag, and what are the consequences?”

content.text: Class imbalance and the accuracy trap
Consider 1,000 payment transactions: 980 legitimate, 20 fraudulent. A useless model predicts every transaction as legitimate.

content.explanation: A 98% accuracy that catches zero fraud.

content.caption: Figure 3. A model can post very high accuracy while failing completely on the minority class.

content.text: Balanced accuracy

content.explanation: Gives equal weight to positive and negative class performance.

content.text: In the “predict everything normal” example, recall = 0% and specificity = 100%, so balanced accuracy = 50% — correctly exposing baseline-level performance.
For imbalanced classification, inspect the confusion matrix and report precision, recall, F1, specificity, balanced accuracy, and ROC-AUC or PR-AUC as appropriate. Never rely on accuracy alone.

content.text: Threshold and matrix changes
Many classifiers first output a probability or score; a threshold converts it into a label. With a threshold of 0.50, scores of 0.50 or more may be labelled positive.

items: Lowering the threshold predicts more positives: TP may rise, but FP may also rise.
Raising the threshold predicts fewer positives: FP may fall, but FN may rise.

content.caption: Figure 4. The conceptual precision–recall trade-off as the classification threshold changes.

content.text: Choose the threshold by the cost of FP and FN, the required precision or recall, and operational constraints — not simply because 0.50 is the default.
content.title: Threshold selection

content.text: Multiclass confusion matrix
A multiclass matrix has one row and column per class. The diagonal still shows correct predictions; off-diagonal cells show which classes get confused with which.

content.caption: Figure 5. A three-class example — cats, dogs and rabbits.

rows: 42 actual cats correctly predicted as cats.
3 actual cats wrongly predicted as dogs.
5 actual dogs wrongly predicted as rabbits.
6 actual rabbits wrongly predicted as dogs.
Dogs and rabbits are confused more than cats and rabbits.

content.text: One-vs-rest interpretation
To get precision or recall for one class, treat that class as “positive” and all others together as “negative.” For the class Dog:

items: TP = Dog predicted as Dog = 36.
FN = actual Dog predicted as Cat or Rabbit = 4 + 5 = 9.
FP = actual Cat or Rabbit predicted as Dog = 3 + 6 = 9.

content.explanation: Here precision and recall coincide because Dog's false positives and false negatives are equal.

content.text: Macro, micro and weighted averages

rows: Metric per class, then an unweighted mean.
Average class metrics weighted by support.
Pool TP, FP, FN across classes, then compute.
Overall instance-level performance is the focus.

content.text: Counts vs normalized matrices
When reporting a normalized matrix, state the normalization method and, ideally, also provide the raw count matrix so readers can see the sample size.

rows: TP, FP, TN, FN may get swapped.
Use rates or normalized matrices too.
Use unseen validation or test data.
FP/FN balance may not suit the task.

content.text: Practical Python example
The key learning point is the sequence: get the true labels, get the predicted labels, then compare them.

content.code:
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix, classification_report

# True labels and model predictions
y_true = [1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0]
y_pred = [1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0]

cm = confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred)
print(cm)   # [[TN, FP], [FN, TP]]

print(classification_report(y_true, y_pred))

content.text: In scikit-learn's standard binary output the array is arranged as [[TN, FP], [FN, TP]] when labels are ordered [0, 1]. Always verify label ordering when using custom labels.

items: Name the positive class and describe the dataset split.
Show the raw confusion matrix with clear axis labels.
State the number of observations in each class (support).
Report accuracy only alongside more diagnostic metrics.
Explain whether false positives or false negatives matter more.
For imbalanced data, include minority-class precision and recall.
For multiclass data, provide per-class and averaged metrics.
State the classification threshold or decision rule.
Compare against a simple baseline model.
Interpret practical consequences, not only percentages.

One row and column per class.

content.text: A confusion matrix is a structured count of correct and incorrect outcomes that reveals not only whether a model is wrong, but how it is wrong.

Find as many positives as possible

content.text: Practice questions
Work through these, then check the answers.

items: A medical model has TP = 80, TN = 900, FP = 30, FN = 20. Find accuracy, precision, recall and specificity. → Accuracy = 980/1030 = 95.1%; precision = 80/110 = 72.7%; recall = 80/100 = 80.0%; specificity = 900/930 = 96.8%.
For a spam filter, which error sends an important legitimate email to spam? → A false positive (a legitimate email predicted as spam).
Why can 98% accuracy be poor for fraud detection? → The model may just predict the majority class, so minority-class recall could be 0%.
If the threshold is lowered, what usually happens to recall and false positives? → Recall usually rises, but false positives usually rise too.
In a multiclass matrix, what do off-diagonal cells represent? → Misclassifications — actual classes predicted as other classes.
When is precision more important than recall? → When false alarms are costly, e.g. blocking legitimate high-value transactions.

content.text: Always write the positive class, matrix orientation, formula and substituted values before reporting the final percentage. This prevents the most common TP/FP/FN/TN mix-ups.
content.title: Final exam tip

keyPoints: A confusion matrix compares actual vs predicted classes; the diagonal is correct, off-diagonal are errors.
Binary has four outcomes — TP, TN, FP, FN — and every metric (accuracy, precision, recall, specificity, F1, NPV) is computed from them.
Precision focuses on false positives, recall on false negatives; F1 balances the two.
Under imbalance accuracy misleads (98% while catching 0% fraud) — use balanced accuracy and per-class metrics.
A multiclass matrix has one row/column per class; use one-vs-rest for per-class metrics and macro/micro/weighted averaging to summarise.

lessons.title: Classification Metrics
lessons.summary: The full metric toolkit: accuracy, precision, recall, specificity and F1 derived from the confusion matrix with worked calculations, why accuracy misleads under imbalance, threshold trade-offs, ROC curves and ROC-AUC, precision–recall curves and average precision, and when to prefer ROC vs PR.

content.text: The big picture

Classification metrics measure how well a model sorts observations into categories — spam/not spam, fraud/not fraud, positive/negative. No single number tells the whole story, because different mistakes carry very different costs. The art is picking the metric that matches what your errors actually cost.

Always start with the confusion matrix. Accuracy, precision, recall, specificity and F1 are all calculated from its four cells; ROC-AUC and the precision–recall curve evaluate performance across many thresholds.
content.title: Key idea

content.text: These notes stay focused on evaluating classification models. Regression metrics, training algorithms and unrelated preprocessing are intentionally excluded.
content.title: Scope

content.text: Core vocabulary

rows: The class of main interest — spam, disease, fraud.
The opposite — not spam, healthy, legitimate.
The probability cut-off that turns a score into a label.
A dataset where one class is much more common.
A number used to evaluate model predictions.

content.text: The confusion matrix
A confusion matrix compares predicted classes with actual ones. It's called “confusion” because it shows exactly where the model confuses one class for another.

rows: Normal email correctly predicted as normal.
Normal email wrongly marked as spam.
Spam wrongly allowed into the inbox.

content.caption: Figure 1. The confusion matrix for a spam classifier: TP = 30, FP = 10, FN = 5, TN = 55.

content.text: Out of 100 emails: TP = 30, FP = 10, FN = 5, TN = 55. The model makes 85 correct and 15 incorrect predictions — these numbers drive every metric below.
content.title: Worked example data

content.text: Accuracy
The proportion of all predictions that are correct.

content.explanation: 85 out of every 100 emails classified correctly — but this doesn't reveal which type of error occurred.

items: Best when: classes are reasonably balanced and false positives and false negatives cost about the same.
Strength: simple and easy to communicate.
Limitation: can look excellent even when the model completely ignores a rare class.

content.text: Precision
Of all the cases predicted positive, how many were actually positive.

content.explanation: Among 40 emails predicted spam, 30 were truly spam — so a quarter of the spam warnings were false alarms.

items: Answers: “When the model predicts positive, how often is it right?”
Use when false positives are costly — blocking an important email, accusing a legitimate transaction of fraud.
Limitation: precision can be inflated by predicting positive only in a few very certain cases, which lowers recall.

content.text: Recall (sensitivity)
Of all the actual positive cases, how many the model successfully found.

content.explanation: The 35 actual spam emails: the model catches 30 and misses 5.

items: Answers: “Of all real positives, how many did the model detect?”
Use when missing a positive is costly — undetected fraud, a missed security threat, a serious condition.
Limitation: very high recall can be reached by labelling many cases positive, producing more false positives.

content.text: Specificity
Of all the actual negative cases, how many the model correctly rejects as negative.

content.explanation: Of 65 normal emails, 55 stay in the inbox and 10 are wrongly sent to spam.

items: Answers: “Of all real negatives, how many were correctly identified?”
Use when avoiding false alarms among negatives matters.
ROC link: False Positive Rate = 1 − Specificity.

content.text: F1-score
The harmonic mean of precision and recall — high only when both are reasonably high.

content.explanation: The harmonic mean drops sharply if either value is low, so one weak metric can't hide.

items: Why harmonic mean? It punishes an extreme imbalance between precision and recall more than a simple average would.
Use when the positive class matters, the data is imbalanced, and both error types count.
Limitation: F1 ignores true negatives, so don't use it alone when negative-class performance matters.

rows: How balanced are precision and recall?

content.caption: Figure 3. A practical starting point for choosing a metric.

content.text: Why accuracy can mislead
A fraud dataset has 1,000 transactions: 980 legitimate and only 20 fraudulent. Compare two models — the table transposes them so each metric reads across.

rows: Finds 16 frauds, misses 4, raises 20 false alarms.

content.caption: Figure 4. The model with lower accuracy is far more useful for detecting fraud.

content.text: For imbalanced classification, never report accuracy alone. Include the confusion matrix and metrics such as precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC or the precision–recall curve.
content.title: Exam highlight

content.text: Threshold and metric trade-offs
Most classifiers first produce a probability or score; a threshold converts it into a class. With a default 0.50 threshold, 0.70 becomes positive and 0.30 becomes negative.

items: Lower threshold: more positives → recall usually rises, but precision and specificity may fall.
Higher threshold: fewer positives → precision and specificity may rise, but recall may fall.
Best threshold: depends on the real cost of false positives and false negatives — not automatically 0.50.

content.caption: Figure 5. Precision, recall and specificity all shift as the decision threshold changes.

content.text: ROC curve and ROC-AUC
The Receiver Operating Characteristic curve plots the True Positive Rate against the False Positive Rate across many thresholds.

content.expression: TPR = Recall = TP / (TP + FN)     and     FPR = FP / (FP + TN) = 1 − Specificity
content.explanation: Each threshold gives one (FPR, TPR) point on the curve.

content.text: The Area Under the ROC Curve — one value between 0 and 1 summarising the model's ability to rank positive examples above negatives.

content.caption: Figure 6. An example ROC curve; the simulated model has ROC-AUC ≈ 0.973.

rows: No ranking ability; like random guessing.
Excellent — still check for leakage and overfitting.

items: Strength: a threshold-independent summary, good for comparing ranking performance.
Caution: ROC-AUC can look optimistic when the negative class is huge, since many false positives still give a small false-positive rate.
Don't confuse: ROC-AUC evaluates ranking across thresholds — it is not accuracy at one chosen threshold.

content.text: Precision–recall curve
A plot of precision against recall across many thresholds, focusing directly on positive-class performance.

content.caption: Figure 7. An example PR curve (AP ≈ 0.939) at 25% positive-class prevalence — the no-skill baseline sits at 0.25.

items: Why useful: it clearly shows the trade-off between finding more positives and keeping positive predictions reliable.
Best use: imbalanced datasets where the positive class is rare and important.
Baseline: the no-skill precision is roughly the positive-class prevalence — if 5% are positive, a random classifier averages ~5% precision.
Summary value: Average Precision (AP) or area under the PR curve — packages compute it differently, so state the exact measure.

content.text: ROC vs PR curve

rows: Quality and coverage of positive predictions
Can look strong when negatives dominate
Usually more informative for rare positives
Pick a threshold; inspect the matrix
Pick a threshold; inspect the matrix

content.text: Use ROC-AUC for broad ranking comparison, especially when classes aren't extremely imbalanced. Prefer the PR curve when the positive class is rare and false positives strongly affect usefulness.
content.title: ROC or PR?

content.text: Common mistakes

rows: Report the confusion matrix and cost-aligned metrics.
Treating precision and recall as the same
Precision starts from predicted positives; recall from actual positives.
Tune the threshold on validation data and real costs.
Comparing models on different test sets
Evaluate all models on the same untouched test set.
Choosing a metric after seeing test results
Choose the primary metric before final testing.
Also inspect specificity, FPR, or the full matrix.
ROC-AUC measures ranking, not calibration or fixed-threshold accuracy.

content.text: Evaluation checklist

items: Define the positive class clearly.
Count TP, TN, FP, FN on an untouched test set.
Calculate accuracy, precision, recall, specificity and F1.
Check whether the class distribution is balanced or imbalanced.
Decide whether false positives or false negatives are more costly.
Plot ROC and PR curves when probability scores are available.
Choose or tune the threshold on validation data, not the final test set.
Report the chosen metric with a plain-language interpretation.

content.text: Revision
Precision looks at Predicted Positives. Recall looks at Real Positives. Specificity looks at Real Negatives.
content.title: Memory trick

content.text: There is no universally best classification metric. The right one matches the class distribution, the positive class, and the real cost of false positives and false negatives.
content.title: Final takeaway

content.text: Practice questions
Use this confusion matrix: TP = 42, TN = 135, FP = 15, FN = 8. Compute each metric, then check the answers.

items: Calculate precision. → 42 / (42 + 15) = 0.737 = 73.7%.
Calculate specificity. → 135 / (135 + 15) = 0.900 = 90.0%.
Calculate F1-score. → 0.785 = 78.5%.
Which metric to prioritise if missing a positive is very costly? → Recall, because false negatives must be minimised.
Why prefer a PR curve when positives are rare? → It focuses on positive predictions and reveals the precision cost of increasing recall.

keyPoints: All confusion-matrix metrics answer different questions: accuracy (overall), precision (positive purity), recall (positive coverage), specificity (negative coverage), F1 (balance).
Precision starts from predicted positives; recall starts from actual positives — they are not interchangeable.
Accuracy misleads under imbalance; report precision, recall, F1 and curves instead.
ROC-AUC summarises ranking across thresholds but can look optimistic when negatives dominate.
Prefer the precision–recall curve (baseline = prevalence) when the positive class is rare and important.
commonMistakes: Reporting accuracy alone on imbalanced data.
Confusing precision with recall.
Assuming 0.50 is always the best threshold.
Reading ROC-AUC as fixed-threshold accuracy or calibrated probability.

lessons.title: False Positives & False Negatives
lessons.summary: The two classification errors in depth: false positives (Type I, false alarms) vs false negatives (Type II, missed detections), where each sits in the confusion matrix, real-world examples and costs, how the threshold trades one for the other, links to precision/recall/specificity/FPR/FNR, and cost-sensitive model choice.

content.text: Two ways to be wrong

A classification model can miss in exactly two ways. It can raise an alarm when nothing is wrong — a false positive — or it can miss a real case that needed attention — a false negative. These two mistakes look similar on a scoreboard but often carry wildly different costs, and telling them apart is the whole point of this lesson.

content.caption: False positive: the model says positive when reality is negative (a legitimate email marked spam). False negative: the model says negative when reality is positive (a spam email reaching the inbox).

content.text: A model can be wrong in two different ways: it may raise an alarm when nothing is wrong (false positive), or miss a real positive case (false negative). These two mistakes often have very different costs.
content.title: The central idea

content.text: The basic setup

In binary classification a model predicts one of two classes. Crucially, “positive” doesn't mean “good” and “negative” doesn't mean “bad” — they only say whether the target condition is present or absent.

rows: The condition of interest is present.
The condition of interest is absent.
The patient does not have the disease.

content.text: The four possible outcomes
Every prediction lands in one of four cells — two correct (on the diagonal) and two errors (off it).

content.caption: Figure 1. A false positive sits in the actual-negative / predicted-positive cell; a false negative sits in the actual-positive / predicted-negative cell.

content.text: False positive (FP)
When the model predicts the positive class but the actual class is negative.

items: Logical form: predicted positive + actually negative = false positive.
Also called a Type I error in statistical hypothesis testing.
It behaves like a false alarm — the model detects something that isn't truly there.

rows: A legitimate email is placed in the spam folder.
A healthy patient is told a screening result is positive.
A valid card transaction is blocked as fraud.
An alarm activates with no intruder present.
A good product is wrongly rejected as defective.

content.text: False negative (FN)
When the model predicts the negative class but the actual class is positive.

items: Logical form: predicted negative + actually positive = false negative.
Also called a Type II error in statistical hypothesis testing.
It behaves like a missed detection — the model fails to spot something that is truly there.

rows: A spam or phishing email reaches the inbox.
A patient with the disease gets a negative result.
The system fails to detect a real intruder.
A defective product is wrongly approved.

content.text: False positive vs false negative
False Positive = “the model shouted YES, but the truth was NO.” False Negative = “the model said NO, but the truth was YES.”
content.title: Memory trick

content.text: Worked numerical example
A classifier evaluates 200 transactions with these outcomes: TP = 52, TN = 118, FP = 18, FN = 12.

content.caption: Figure 2. Illustrative results across 200 cases: TP = 52, TN = 118, FP = 18, FN = 12.

rows: 13.2% of actual negatives wrongly flagged positive.
74.3% of positive predictions were truly positive.

content.text: Relationship with metrics

items: More false positives usually reduce precision — a larger share of positive predictions is wrong.
More false positives also reduce specificity and raise the false-positive rate.
More false negatives reduce recall (sensitivity) — more actual positives are missed.
A model can have high accuracy yet a harmful number of false negatives when the positive class is rare.
The best metric depends on which mistake carries the greater real-world cost.

content.text: Accuracy alone can hide classification errors. Always inspect the confusion matrix and choose metrics that reflect the business, safety or clinical objective.
content.title: Important caution

content.text: Threshold and the error trade-off

Many classifiers output a probability score, and a threshold converts it into a class. With a threshold of 0.50, a predicted probability of 0.72 becomes positive while 0.31 becomes negative. Move the threshold and the two error counts move in opposite directions.

content.caption: Figure 3. Raising the threshold usually decreases false positives but increases false negatives — the two curves cross near the default 0.50.

content.text: Choosing a threshold

items: Start from the cost of each error, not just the default 0.50.
Use validation data to compare FPR, FNR, precision and recall at several thresholds.
For high-risk screening, a lower threshold may be preferred to reduce missed cases.
For costly investigations or customer disruption, a higher threshold may reduce false alarms.
Document the final threshold and why it supports the application objective.

content.text: Which error is more serious?
There's no universal answer — it depends entirely on the application and the cost of the mistake.

rows: A real disease may be missed and treatment delayed.
An important legitimate email may be hidden.
FP annoys customers; FN causes financial loss.
A real threat may pass undetected.
FP wastes good products; FN releases defective ones.
A real fire may not trigger an alarm.

content.text: Cost-sensitive thinking
A simple way to compare models is to assign an approximate cost to each error and total it up.

content.expression: Total cost = (FP × cost of FP) + (FN × cost of FN)
content.explanation: Weight each error by how much it actually hurts.

content.text: If one false positive costs 2 units and one false negative costs 20 units: a model with 30 FP and 5 FN costs (30×2) + (5×20) = 160 units, while a model with 10 FP and 10 FN costs (10×2) + (10×20) = 220 units. The first model is cheaper even though it makes more total mistakes.
content.title: Worked example

content.text: Common misunderstandings

rows: Positive only means the target condition was predicted present.
Their costs depend on the application.
Accuracy can hide errors when classes are imbalanced.
The threshold should match the required trade-off and cost.
Often a trade-off: reducing FP can increase FN, and vice versa.

content.text: Practice scenarios
Identify whether each situation is a false positive or a false negative, then check your answers.

items: A bank blocks a genuine purchase because the model predicts fraud. → False positive: fraud predicted, transaction genuine.
A disease-screening model reports “healthy” for a patient who has the disease. → False negative: disease present, prediction negative.
A smoke detector sounds because of steam, with no fire. → False positive: fire predicted, none present.
A defective product passes inspection and ships. → False negative: defect present, not detected.
A normal message is moved into the spam folder. → False positive: spam predicted, message legitimate.

content.text: Revision

items: A false positive is a positive prediction for an actually negative case.
A false negative is a negative prediction for an actually positive case.
False positives are false alarms; false negatives are missed detections.
The confusion matrix shows the exact counts of both errors.
Raising the threshold usually reduces FP but increases FN; lowering it does the reverse.
The best model and threshold depend on the relative cost of the two error types.
Examine precision, recall, specificity, FPR and FNR — not accuracy alone.

content.text: False positive: predicted YES, truth NO. False negative: predicted NO, truth YES.

rows: The true label of an observation.
The label assigned by the model.
The event or condition the model is designed to detect.
The probability cut-off used to convert a score into a class.
Proportion of actual negatives wrongly predicted positive.
Proportion of actual positives wrongly predicted negative.
Proportion of actual positives correctly detected.
Proportion of actual negatives correctly identified.

keyPoints: A false positive predicts positive when the truth is negative (Type I, false alarm); a false negative predicts negative when the truth is positive (Type II, missed detection).
False positives hurt precision and specificity; false negatives hurt recall/sensitivity.
Raising the threshold usually cuts false positives but adds false negatives; lowering it does the reverse.
Which error is worse depends entirely on the application and the cost of the mistake.
Compare models by expected cost (FP×cost + FN×cost), not by total error count alone.

Treating false positives and false negatives as equally harmful.
