lessons.title: Choosing Suitable Metrics
lessons.summary: A practical guide to selecting evaluation metrics that match the task, data, error costs and real objective: a seven-step framework, decision tables for classification (accuracy, precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, MCC) and regression (MAE, RMSE, R², MAPE), probability/ranking metrics, the primary-plus-guardrails pattern, worked examples, and a selection checklist.

content.text: Why metric choice matters

There is no single metric that wins every machine-learning problem. The right one is whichever number most closely tracks the real objective — the actual cost of getting a decision wrong. Pick the wrong metric and a model can look brilliant on paper while failing completely in practice.
A numerical measure used to judge how well a model performs on unseen data. A suitable metric is one whose meaning closely matches the real objective of the problem.
Model selection should optimise the outcome that matters — not merely the metric that produces the largest-looking number.
content.title: Key idea

content.text: These notes stay focused on choosing suitable evaluation metrics. Definitions appear only where they help metric selection.
content.title: Scope

content.caption: A quick map of scenario → typical primary metric: balanced labels → accuracy, rare positives → PR-AUC/F1, high FN cost → recall, high FP cost → precision, calibrated probabilities → log loss/Brier, large errors critical → RMSE/MSE.

content.text: What goes wrong without it

rows: A fraud model reports 99% accuracy but misses most fraud.
Accuracy is dominated by the majority class.
Missing cancer vs an extra test.
Recall may deserve priority over precision.
$100 error: fine for a house, severe for a cheap product.
Absolute and percentage errors tell different stories.
A few extreme errors dominate MSE/RMSE.
MAE may better describe typical performance.

content.text: A seven-step selection framework
A repeatable process keeps metric choice honest and defensible.

content.caption: Figure 1. A repeatable process for selecting and validating ML metrics.

items: Identify the task — classification or regression?
Identify the goal — correct labels, rare cases, small errors, or probabilities?
Check the data — balanced classes? outliers? zero or negative targets?
Compare error costs — which mistake is worse, a false positive or a false negative?
Select the primary metric that directly represents the real objective.
Add 1–3 guardrail metrics to prevent a misleading conclusion.
Validate across folds and subgroups — report mean, variation, and a confusion matrix or error plot.

content.text: Metrics for classification

Classification predicts a category — positive/negative, spam/not spam, or one of several classes. The choice hinges on class balance and the consequences of false positives (FP) and false negatives (FN).

content.caption: Figure 2. The confusion-matrix outcomes that underpin most classification metrics.

content.text: Essential formulas

content.explanation: Overall fraction correct — best when classes and error costs are reasonably balanced.
Of predicted positives, the fraction truly positive — choose when false positives are costly.
Of actual positives, the fraction detected — choose when false negatives are costly.
Of actual negatives, the fraction correctly rejected — useful when avoiding false alarms matters.
Harmonic mean of precision and recall — useful when both matter and the positive class is important.

content.text: Classification metric decision table

rows: Can hide failure on a rare class
Doesn't show if FP or FN is the issue
Can be high while missing many positives
Can rise by adding false alarms
Ignores TN; assumes equal P/R importance
Harder to explain to non-technical audiences

content.text: When the positive class is rare, use a class-sensitive metric — recall, precision, F1, PR-AUC, balanced accuracy or MCC. Keep accuracy only as a supporting metric.
content.title: Selection rule

content.text: Accuracy and class imbalance

content.caption: Figure 3. A model can reach high accuracy while completely missing the minority class.

content.text: Precision vs recall in practice

rows: Catch true cases; follow-up handles extra FPs.
Match a threshold to investigation capacity.
Detection is critical, but limit false alarms.

content.text: Thresholds change metric values

A probability classifier becomes a label classifier only after a threshold is chosen. Raising the threshold usually raises precision and lowers recall; lowering it does the reverse. So pick the threshold using the primary metric and real operating constraints.

content.caption: Figure 4. The precision–recall–F1 trade-off as the decision threshold changes.

content.text: AUC compares ranking across thresholds, but deployment uses one operating threshold. Always report performance at the chosen threshold too.
content.title: Important

content.text: Worked classification example
A model evaluates 1,000 cases: TP = 80, TN = 860, FP = 40, FN = 20.

Interpretation: the model rejects negatives well, but one-third of its positive alerts are false. If missed positives cost most, make recall primary; if false alerts consume expensive expert time, emphasise precision.
Metrics for regression
Regression predicts a continuous value — price, temperature, demand, duration. The choice depends on whether typical error, large error, relative error, or explained variation matters most.

rows: Typical absolute error should be clear
Large errors must be punished; training loss
Large errors matter, keep target units
Dominated by a few extreme errors
Variance explained vs a mean baseline
Hides error size; can be negative
Percentage error; positive targets away from 0
Need a more symmetric relative error
Reduces effect of very large targets

content.text: Choose MAE for a clear “average error” and greater robustness. Choose RMSE/MSE when large mistakes are disproportionately costly. Report both when tail errors are operationally important.
content.title: Selection rule

content.text: MAE vs RMSE/MSE

content.caption: Figure 5. A large error contributes far more to MSE than to MAE — the squared penalty explodes for the biggest mistake.

content.text: Worked regression example
Actual values [100, 120, 140, 160] and predictions [110, 115, 150, 130] give errors [10, −5, 10, −30].

RMSE exceeds MAE because the 30-unit error gets a strong squared penalty. If a 30-unit mistake causes serious cost, RMSE is a suitable primary metric; if you want to describe the typical error a user faces, MAE communicates it more clearly.
When percentage metrics fail

items: Don't use MAPE when actual values can be zero — division by zero is undefined.
Be cautious when values are near zero — tiny denominators create enormous percentages.
Don't use standard percentage-error metrics with negative targets unless carefully adapted.
For mixed scales, use MAE/RMSE with a normalised companion, or evaluate by target range.

content.text: Metrics for probabilities and ranking
Some models produce probability estimates or rankings rather than a final yes/no. Label metrics alone may not be enough.

rows: A model can rank well yet be badly calibrated.
Focus on the top portion actually reviewed.
Choose k to match the visible/actionable list.

content.text: One primary metric plus guardrails
A strong evaluation plan names one primary metric for model selection and a small set of supporting guardrails. This prevents “metric shopping” and exposes hidden weaknesses.

rows: Recall at fixed precision; precision at capacity; calibration
Specificity; precision; false negatives by subgroup
RMSE; R²; error by price band
RMSE; bias/mean error; error by product category

content.text: State the primary metric before comparing models, explain why it matches the objective, and report uncertainty across validation folds or repeated runs.
content.title: Good reporting practice

content.text: Quick selection guide

rows: Log loss or Brier plus calibration
MAPE/sMAPE only when safely above zero
R² as a supporting metric, not alone

content.text: Common mistakes

rows: Check class distribution and error costs first.
Add confusion-matrix parts, error plots, subgroup results.
Select on validation/CV; test once for final evaluation.
Only compare under comparable data, splits, prevalence.
Set the threshold by business/clinical constraints.
Also report an error metric in the target unit.
Choose MAE, RMSE, WAPE, or a stable alternative.
Check for weak performance on important groups.
Report CV mean and standard deviation or CI.

content.text: Justifying a metric
A clear justification connects the metric to the decision. Two worked examples:

Fraud detection: “PR-AUC was selected as the primary metric because fraudulent transactions were rare and positive-class retrieval was the central objective. Precision and recall at the final threshold were also reported to show the trade-off between investigation workload and missed fraud.”
content.title: Example — classification

content.text: House-price regression: “MAE was selected as the primary metric because it expresses the typical prediction error in the same unit as house price and is less dominated by extreme properties than squared-error metrics. RMSE and R² were included as supporting metrics to identify large-error sensitivity and explained variance.”
content.title: Example — regression

content.text: Reusable structure: “The primary metric was [metric] because [error/goal] was the main concern. [Supporting metrics] were also reported to monitor [secondary risks]. This was appropriate because [class balance, target scale, threshold, or operational constraint].”
content.title: Template

content.text: Selection checklist

items: What type of prediction: class label, probability, ranking, or continuous value?
What real decision will be made using the prediction?
Which error is more costly: FP, FN, small numeric error, or large numeric error?
Are the classes imbalanced or the target values highly skewed?
Are zero, negative, or extreme target values present?
Does the metric have an interpretation stakeholders can understand?
Will a threshold or top-k capacity be used in deployment?
Have one primary metric and a few guardrails been declared before comparison?
Are results reported across validation folds and important subgroups?
Is the final test set kept separate from metric and threshold selection?

content.text: Key takeaways

items: The best metric represents the real cost or objective of the application.
Accuracy is suitable only when class balance and error costs make it meaningful.
Precision and recall follow the relative cost of false positives and false negatives.
PR-AUC is often more informative than ROC-AUC when the positive class is rare.
MAE describes typical regression error; RMSE/MSE emphasise large errors.
R² and AUC should be supported by threshold-specific or unit-based metrics.
Use one primary metric, supporting guardrails, cross-validation uncertainty, and subgroup checks.

content.text: Choose metrics by connecting the model's errors to the real consequences of the decision, then verify that the chosen score doesn't hide important failure modes.
content.title: One-sentence summary

keyPoints: No metric is universally best — choose the one whose meaning matches the real cost or objective of the decision.
For classification, let class balance and FP/FN costs drive the choice; use class-sensitive metrics (recall, precision, F1, PR-AUC, MCC) when positives are rare.
For regression, MAE describes typical error while RMSE/MSE emphasise large errors; avoid MAPE near zero or negative targets.
Declare one primary metric plus 1–3 guardrails before comparing models, and report at the deployed threshold, not just AUC.
Validate across folds and subgroups and keep the final test set separate from metric and threshold selection.
commonMistakes: Defaulting to accuracy without checking class balance and error costs.
Selecting the metric or threshold on the test set.
Reporting a single number without guardrails, uncertainty, or subgroup checks.
Using MAPE when targets can be zero or negative.

lessons.title: Practical Project: Disease Classification
lessons.summary: An end-to-end binary-classification capstone on the public Breast Cancer Wisconsin dataset: defining the problem and positive class, leakage-safe splitting and pipelines, EDA, four candidate models compared by risk-sensitive metrics, confusion matrix and ROC/PR analysis, threshold trade-offs, feature importance, full reproducible scikit-learn code, and the ethics of medical ML.

content.text: A complete classification project

This capstone walks through a full binary-classification project end to end — from defining the question to evaluating errors and discussing ethics — using a public dataset. The task: tell malignant from benign breast-mass samples. Everything here is for learning the workflow, not for making real medical decisions.

This project demonstrates machine-learning concepts. It must not be used to diagnose, treat, or decide anything about a real patient. Clinical systems require validated medical evidence, regulatory approval, external testing, and qualified professional oversight.
content.title: Important safety note

content.caption: An educational schematic of regular (benign) vs irregular (malignant) cell patterns — not a medical image and not suitable for diagnosis.

content.text: Project overview

Disease classification is a supervised learning task: a model learns from labelled examples and predicts a discrete health-related class for a new observation. Here the two classes are malignant and benign.
Can measurements extracted from digitized images of breast-mass cell nuclei help a model distinguish malignant from benign samples?

rows: A measured characteristic of cell nuclei.
The known class used in training.
The model's estimated class or probability.
Cut-off that turns a probability into a class.

content.text: Why it's a binary classification problem

items: Two classes: each sample is malignant or benign.
Labelled examples: the correct diagnosis is available for training and evaluation.
Probabilistic output: many classifiers can estimate a probability for the malignant class.
Asymmetric errors: missing a malignant case is usually more serious than flagging a benign case for review.

content.text: The public dataset

rows: UCI ML Repository; also bundled in scikit-learn.
Measurements from digitized fine-needle aspirate images.

content.caption: Figure 1. The dataset is moderately imbalanced: 357 benign (62.7%) vs 212 malignant (37.3%).

content.text: The goal is not to teach breast-cancer medicine. The dataset is used only as a clear, public example for learning the classification workflow.
content.title: Keep the task relevant

content.text: How the 30 features are organised
Ten basic cell-nucleus measurements are each recorded in three forms — mean, standard error, and “worst” (largest/most extreme) value — giving 10 × 3 = 30 features.

rows: Average distance from centre to perimeter.
Shape compactness from perimeter and area.

content.text: The end-to-end workflow

content.caption: Figure 2. The practical classification workflow — a reliable project is a repeatable pipeline, not just a high accuracy score.

Load the dataset and confirm rows, columns, target labels, and data types.
Explore class balance, summary statistics, outliers, and feature relationships.
Split into training and test sets before learning any preprocessing parameters.

Interpret probabilities, thresholds, errors, and influential features.
Document limitations and avoid presenting the result as a clinical tool.

content.text: Data leakage: the rule that protects honest evaluation
When information from the test set, future data, or the target indirectly influences training — making performance look better than it will be in real use.

rows: Scale the full dataset, then split.
Split first; fit the scaler on training data only.
Tune the model using the final test set.
Select features by looking at all labels.
Do feature selection inside a pipeline/folds.
Report only the best random split.
Fix the seed and use cross-validation for stability.

content.text: Exploratory data analysis
The benign class has 357 samples (62.7%) and the malignant class 212 (37.3%). Accuracy alone can therefore hide important errors, so a stratified split keeps both sets at similar class proportions.

content.caption: Figure 3. A stratified 80/20 split: 455 training samples and 114 test samples, preserving class proportions.

content.text: Feature patterns
Group averages differ clearly between classes — malignant nuclei tend to be larger and more irregular.

content.caption: Figure 4. Mean radius vs mean texture show partial class separation, but overlap remains — which motivates multivariable models.

content.text: A difference in group averages does not prove causation and does not mean one feature can diagnose a sample. The model combines patterns across many features.

rows: Makes malignant the positive class for recall/precision.
Preserves proportions; keeps an unseen test set.
Standardize for Logistic Regression and SVM.
Decision Tree and Random Forest use raw features.
Tree splits aren't sensitive to units the same way.
Gives more attention to the rarer malignant class.
Makes split and stochastic behaviour repeatable.

content.expression: z = (x − training mean) / training standard deviation
content.explanation: After standardization, a value describes how many training standard deviations it sits from the training mean. Test values must be transformed with the training mean and standard deviation, never their own.

The training set is judged with stratified five-fold cross-validation — each model trains five times, each fold validates once — before the untouched test set is used.

Strong on scaled, medium numeric data.
RBF kernel; StandardScaler; probability=True; balanced weights.

content.text: Evaluation metrics
Malignant is the positive class, so a false negative means an actual malignant sample was predicted benign — the highest-risk error here.

content.explanation: Overall proportion correct — a useful summary, but insufficient when errors differ in consequence.
Of samples predicted malignant, the proportion truly malignant. Low precision means many false alarms.
Of actual malignant samples, the proportion detected. Low recall means malignant cases are missed.
Of actual benign samples, the proportion correctly identified as benign.
Harmonic mean of precision and recall — useful when both errors matter.

content.text: ROC-AUC measures how well the model ranks malignant cases above benign across thresholds; average precision summarises the precision–recall curve, and is especially informative for the rarer positive class.
Model results

These values come from the fixed 20% test set (114 samples). They are useful for learning but are not evidence of clinical performance — the dataset is small, historical, and not externally validated. The 6-column results are split into two tables so they read cleanly on a phone.

content.caption: Figure 5. On this split the SVM gives the highest test recall with a strong balance of precision and F1.

content.text: The SVM is selected for the remaining evaluation because it reached 0.976 recall, 0.976 precision, and 0.995 ROC-AUC on the test split. Logistic Regression is a close and more interpretable alternative.

content.text: Cross-validation check

The cross-validation ranking is not identical to the test-set ranking — normal for a small dataset with sampling variation. The lesson: compare several metrics and examine stability, don't pick a model from one number.
Understanding the selected model

content.caption: Figure 6. Test confusion matrix: 71 true negatives, 1 false positive, 1 false negative, 41 true positives.

rows: Benign predicted malignant — unnecessary extra review.
Malignant predicted benign — the highest-risk error.

content.text: A model with excellent accuracy can still be unacceptable if it misses too many malignant cases. Always inspect the false-negative count and recall when the positive class represents serious risk.

content.text: ROC and precision–recall curves

content.caption: Figure 7a. The ROC curve plots recall against false-positive rate across thresholds (SVM ROC-AUC = 0.995).
Figure 7b. The precision–recall curve focuses on positive-class detection (average precision = 0.994; prevalence = 0.368).

items: ROC curve: recall vs false-positive rate — curves closer to the top-left are better.
Precision–recall curve: how precision changes with recall — directly focuses on positive-class detection.
High AUC does not select a threshold — the final threshold must reflect the cost of FNs and FPs.

content.text: Thresholds and decision trade-offs
A classifier first produces a probability; the threshold turns it into a class. At the default 0.50, probabilities ≥ 0.50 are predicted malignant.

content.caption: Figure 8. Changing the threshold changes precision, recall, and specificity — the relationship must be evaluated for the intended use.

rows: More predicted malignant; recall may rise, FPs increase.
Fewer predicted malignant; precision/specificity may rise.

content.text: The best threshold is not automatically 0.50. It should be chosen with clinicians, validation data, resource constraints, and an explicit statement of which errors cost more. This educational split is far too small for a real threshold decision.
content.title: Threshold selection is a policy decision

content.text: Feature importance and interpretation

content.caption: Figure 9. Random-forest impurity importance highlights the features that contributed most to its splits (worst perimeter, worst area, concave points…).

items: Feature importance is model-specific — another model or sample can rank differently.
Importance is not causation — a feature can predict without causing the disease.
Correlated features share information — radius, perimeter and area are related, so importance can split or inflate.
Global importance is not an individual explanation — explaining one prediction needs local methods and clinical context.

content.text: Use feature importance to understand model behaviour and detect suspicious shortcuts. Do not present it as a medical explanation of why a patient has a disease.

content.text: Complete compact project script

content.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, StratifiedKFold, cross_validate
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report, confusion_matrix, roc_auc_score

# 1) Data
data = load_breast_cancer(as_frame=True)
X = data.data
y = (data.target == 0).astype(int)   # 1 = malignant

# 2) Honest split
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.20, stratify=y, random_state=42
)

# 3) Pipeline
model = Pipeline([
    ("scale", StandardScaler()),
    ("svm", SVC(
        kernel="rbf", probability=True,
        class_weight="balanced", random_state=42
    ))
])

# 4) Cross-validation on training data
cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
scores = cross_validate(
    model, X_train, y_train, cv=cv,
    scoring=["accuracy", "precision", "recall", "f1", "roc_auc"]
)
for metric in ["accuracy", "precision", "recall", "f1", "roc_auc"]:
    print(metric, np.mean(scores[f"test_{metric}"]))

# 5) Final test evaluation
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
prob = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
pred = (prob >= 0.50).astype(int)
print(classification_report(y_test, pred, target_names=["benign", "malignant"]))
print(confusion_matrix(y_test, pred))
print("ROC-AUC:", roc_auc_score(y_test, prob))

content.text: Ethical and deployment requirements

items: Privacy: health data must be protected, minimised, de-identified where appropriate, and governed clearly.
Fairness: check performance across demographic and clinical subgroups — an overall score can hide harmful disparities.
Human oversight: qualified professionals should review outputs, especially uncertain and high-risk cases.
Explainability: users need understandable reasons, uncertainty information, and known limitations.
Monitoring: track data drift, device changes, population changes, and failure rates after deployment.
Regulatory compliance: clinical decision-support may be regulated as medical software, needing formal quality and safety processes.

content.text: The WDBC dataset is useful for teaching, but it is small and historical. A high score on one split does not establish safety, generalizability, fairness, or clinical benefit.

content.text: Key takeaways

items: A practical project begins with a precise target and error definition, not with an algorithm.
Public datasets are valuable for learning, but their scope and age limit real-world conclusions.
Pipelines prevent leakage by fitting preprocessing only on training data.
Accuracy must be supported by recall, precision, F1, confusion matrix, ROC-AUC, and PR analysis.
Threshold choice changes the balance between missed malignant cases and false alarms.
Interpretability shows model behaviour; it does not provide biological causation.
Medical ML requires external validation, fairness checks, privacy, monitoring, regulation, and human oversight.

content.title: One-sentence summary

keyPoints: Start from a precise target and error definition (malignant = positive) before choosing an algorithm.
Prevent leakage with a stratified split and pipelines that fit preprocessing on training data only.
Judge a risk-sensitive classifier by recall, precision, F1, confusion matrix and ROC/PR — never accuracy alone.
The threshold is a policy decision balancing missed malignant cases against false alarms; 0.50 is just a default.
A strong score on one small historical split is not clinical readiness — medical ML needs external validation, fairness, privacy, monitoring and human oversight.
commonMistakes: Using accuracy alone and hiding false negatives.
Scaling or selecting features before the train–test split.
Repeatedly checking the test set until it becomes tuning data.
Presenting a probability score as a clinical diagnosis.
